competition_description:
Molecular Atom Index Prediction: Identifying Scalar Coupling Atom Positions

In the study of molecular structure and Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, understanding the precise positioning of atoms within a molecule is critical for predicting scalar coupling constants and other molecular properties. This competition challenges participants to predict the index of the first atom (atom_index_0) involved in a scalar coupling pair, given molecular structural features, bond types, and chemical properties derived from quantum mechanical calculations.

The dataset is derived from the CHAMPS scalar coupling dataset, containing information about molecular geometries, atom types, coupling types, and various structural descriptors. Participants must leverage these features to accurately regress the atom index value, which represents the positional identifier of the first atom in a scalar coupling interaction. The target variable ranges from 3 to 22, with a mean of approximately 10.5, reflecting the diversity of molecular sizes and atom arrangements present in the dataset.

This task has practical implications for automated molecular structure analysis and NMR spectrum interpretation pipelines. Accurate prediction of atom indices can assist in automating the assignment of NMR peaks to specific atomic positions within complex molecules, potentially accelerating drug discovery and materials science research.

Submissions are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE). This metric is calculated as the square root of the mean of the squared differences between the logarithm of predicted values plus one and the logarithm of actual values plus one. RMSLE penalizes under-predictions more than over-predictions and is robust to the effect of large outliers, making it suitable for this positively-valued regression target.

competition_description:
Elo Merchant Feature Prediction: Classify Customer Transaction Feature

Elo, one of the largest payment brands in Brazil, has built extensive partnerships with merchants to offer personalized promotions and discounts to cardholders. Understanding the characteristics of these transactions and the merchants involved is critical to delivering the right experience to the right customer at the right time. In this competition, participants are challenged to predict a key binary merchant feature (feature_3) based on transaction and card-level data derived from Elo's loyalty program dataset.

The target variable, feature_3, is a binary indicator associated with merchant or transaction characteristics that plays a role in how Elo segments and targets its customer base. By accurately predicting this feature, data scientists can help Elo better understand the underlying patterns in merchant categorization, ultimately contributing to more effective and personalized recommendation systems. Participants will work with anonymized transaction histories, card-level attributes, and merchant metadata to build robust classification models.

This challenge is ideal for practitioners interested in real-world financial transaction data, feature engineering on behavioral signals, and binary classification in a noisy, imbalanced environment. Strong solutions will leverage creative feature construction and well-calibrated probabilistic predictions.

Submissions are evaluated using the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). The AUC metric measures the ability of the model to distinguish between the two classes (feature_3 = 0 vs feature_3 = 1) across all classification thresholds. A score of 1.0 represents a perfect classifier, while a score of 0.5 represents random guessing. Higher AUC scores indicate better model performance.

competition_description:
Elo Cardholder Feature Classification Challenge

Elo, one of the largest payment brands in Brazil, collects various anonymized features about its cardholders to better understand customer behavior and improve personalized recommendations. In this competition, your task is to predict a key categorical cardholder attribute — `feature_1` — using transaction history, merchant data, and other cardholder-level information. This feature is believed to encode important segmentation information about Elo's customer base.

Participants will leverage rich historical transaction data, including merchant category details, purchase amounts, and temporal patterns, to classify each cardholder into one of five categories (1 through 5) for `feature_1`. Understanding this attribute can help Elo better tailor promotions and discount campaigns to the right customer segments, ultimately improving customer satisfaction and merchant engagement.

This is a multi-class classification problem. You are encouraged to explore feature engineering from transaction-level data, aggregation strategies, and advanced machine learning techniques to build the most accurate probabilistic classifier possible.

Submissions are evaluated using **multi-class logarithmic loss (log loss)**. For each card_id in the test set, you must predict the probability that the cardholder belongs to each of the five classes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) for `feature_1`. Lower log loss values indicate better model performance. The formula penalizes confident but incorrect predictions heavily, so well-calibrated probability estimates are essential.

competition_description:
Ames Housing: Predict Type 2 Finished Basement Square Footage

When evaluating a residential property, the details of basement finishing can significantly impact a home's utility and value. This competition challenges you to predict the Type 2 finished basement square footage (BsmtFinSF2) for residential homes in Ames, Iowa, using a rich dataset of 79 explanatory variables describing nearly every aspect of each property.

The target variable, BsmtFinSF2, represents the square footage of a second type of finished basement area. As reflected in the data, the majority of homes have no Type 2 finished basement space (with 75% of values at 0), making this a challenging regression task with a heavily zero-inflated distribution and a maximum value of 1,127 square feet. Competitors must leverage features such as overall basement dimensions, construction quality, neighborhood characteristics, and other structural attributes to accurately predict this niche but informative property feature.

This competition is ideal for practitioners looking to sharpen their skills in handling skewed distributions, zero-inflated targets, and feature engineering on structured tabular data. Explore creative approaches to feature selection and model building to rise to the top of the leaderboard.

Submissions are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) between the predicted and actual Type 2 finished basement square footage values. RMSE is calculated as the square root of the average squared differences between predicted and observed values. Lower RMSE scores indicate better model performance.

competition_description:
PlantClimates 2024: Predicting Seasonal Precipitation Variability from Plant Photographs

This competition challenges participants to predict a key climate variable — the delta precipitation between the wettest and driest months (WORLDCLIM BIO13-BIO14) — from citizen science plant photographs. This metric captures the degree of seasonal precipitation variability at a plant's location, ranging from near-uniform rainfall year-round to highly seasonal climates with extreme wet and dry periods. Understanding this relationship can help us infer local climate conditions from plant imagery alone, opening new possibilities for large-scale environmental monitoring.

Plants are exquisite indicators of their environment. The species present, their morphology, and even the visual texture of their leaves and stems carry embedded signals about the climate they inhabit. By learning to decode these signals from photographs collected through citizen science platforms like iNaturalist, we can potentially reconstruct fine-grained climate information at a global scale. This competition provides a curated dataset of plant images paired with geolocated climate measurements, enabling participants to build models that bridge visual ecology and climatology.

Participants are encouraged to leverage deep learning, transfer learning, and any additional tabular or metadata features provided alongside the images. The target variable spans a wide range (approximately 3 to 1290 mm), reflecting the diversity of climatic zones represented in the dataset. Creative feature engineering and robust modeling approaches will be key to achieving strong performance on this challenging regression task.

Submissions are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE). This metric is appropriate given the wide range and right-skewed distribution of the target variable, as it penalizes under-predictions more heavily than over-predictions and reduces the influence of very large values. A lower RMSLE indicates better model performance. The formula is: RMSLE = sqrt( (1/n) * sum( (log(predicted + 1) - log(actual + 1))^2 ) ).

competition_description:
Predicting Soil Organic Carbon from Citizen Science Plant Photographs

Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a critical indicator of soil health, ecosystem productivity, and carbon sequestration capacity. Understanding the spatial distribution of SOC is essential for climate change mitigation strategies and sustainable land management. This competition challenges participants to predict near-surface soil organic carbon content (at 5-15cm depth, measured in mg/kg) from citizen science plant photographs and associated metadata, leveraging the intimate relationship between vegetation and soil properties.

The dataset is derived from the PlantTraits2024 collection, pairing geolocated citizen science plant images from platforms such as iNaturalist and Pl@ntNet with corresponding soil organic carbon measurements from high-resolution global soil databases. Plants both reflect and influence the organic carbon content of the soils they grow in — decomposing plant matter is the primary source of soil organic carbon, while SOC-rich soils support denser and more diverse vegetation. By training models on plant photographs and ancillary environmental features, participants aim to build a scalable, cost-effective approach to mapping soil carbon across diverse ecosystems.

This task has significant real-world implications: traditional SOC measurements require expensive and time-consuming soil sampling campaigns, whereas citizen science photographs are already available in the millions globally. A successful model could enable rapid, large-scale SOC estimation to support carbon accounting, agricultural planning, and ecosystem monitoring efforts worldwide.

Submissions are evaluated using the Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE). This metric is appropriate given the wide range and right-skewed distribution of SOC values, as it penalizes under-predictions and over-predictions more equally on a relative scale. RMSLE is computed as: RMSLE = sqrt( (1/n) * sum( (log(predicted + 1) - log(actual + 1))^2 ) ). Lower values indicate better model performance.

competition_description:
PlantSnap Climate: Predicting Annual Precipitation from Citizen Science Plant Photos

Can a photograph of a plant tell you how much rain falls where it lives? This competition challenges participants to predict annual precipitation (WORLDCLIM BIO12) at plant observation sites using citizen science plant photographs and associated metadata. Plants are exquisitely adapted to their local climate, and their visual appearance — leaf texture, color, morphology, and growth form — often reflects the moisture regime of their environment. By learning these visual and contextual signals, models may unlock a powerful new way to infer climatic conditions from biodiversity data.

Participants are provided with tens of thousands of georeferenced plant photographs collected through citizen science platforms, along with ancillary plant trait measurements and environmental covariates. The target variable, WORLDCLIM BIO12 annual precipitation, ranges from near-desert conditions (~16 mm/year) to extremely wet tropical environments (~4300 mm/year), presenting a challenging regression task across a wide dynamic range. Successful models will need to capture both the visual cues encoded in plant images and the statistical relationships between plant traits and precipitation regimes.

This task has real-world relevance for global change research: understanding how plant communities reflect and respond to precipitation gradients is critical for monitoring ecosystem shifts under climate change. Models developed here could help scientists infer local climate conditions from the rapidly growing archive of citizen science plant observations, even in regions where direct climate measurements are sparse.

Submissions are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE). This metric is appropriate given the wide range of precipitation values and ensures that errors on lower precipitation values are penalized proportionally to errors on higher values. RMSLE is calculated as: RMSLE = sqrt( (1/n) * sum( (log(predicted + 1) - log(actual + 1))^2 ) ). Lower RMSLE values indicate better model performance.

competition_description:
Ventilator Inspiratory Control Signal Prediction

Mechanical ventilation is a critical procedure used to assist patients who cannot breathe on their own. A ventilator delivers air to a patient's lungs by controlling two key signals: the inspiratory solenoid valve control (u_in) and the expiratory valve control (u_out). Accurately predicting the inspiratory control signal (u_in) is essential for understanding and simulating how ventilators respond to varying lung conditions, characterized by compliance (C) and resistance (R).

In this competition, your task is to predict the u_in signal — the control input to the inspiratory solenoid valve — given time-series data from a simulated ventilator connected to a lung model. The dataset contains breath-by-breath recordings including time steps, lung attributes, pressure readings, and the expiratory valve state. Your models must generalize across different lung configurations, capturing the continuous variability in patient lung characteristics.

This challenge mirrors real-world difficulties in ventilator control research: building parametric models that adapt to diverse patient physiologies. Successful solutions could contribute to the development of smarter, more adaptive ventilation algorithms, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving patient outcomes in critical care settings.

Submissions are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) between the predicted and actual u_in values. RMSE is defined as the square root of the mean of squared differences between predicted and observed values. Lower RMSE scores indicate better model performance.

competition_description:
Ventilator Lung Compliance Classification

Mechanical ventilation is a critical procedure used to support patients who cannot breathe on their own. A key parameter governing how a ventilator interacts with a patient's lungs is **compliance (C)** — a measure of the lung's ability to stretch and expand. Understanding and predicting lung compliance from ventilator sensor readings is essential for personalizing ventilation strategies and improving patient outcomes. In this competition, you are challenged to classify the lung compliance setting of a simulated ventilator system using time-series sensor data collected during breathing cycles.

The dataset contains sequences of ventilator readings including airway pressure, flow, and control signals recorded across many breath cycles. Each breath sequence is associated with a specific lung compliance value (C), which takes discrete values of 10, 20, or 50. Your task is to build a model that accurately identifies the compliance class from the observed sensor data. This mirrors a real-world clinical scenario where clinicians must infer patient lung characteristics from observable ventilator measurements to optimize treatment.

Successful models in this competition could contribute to the development of smarter, adaptive ventilator control systems that automatically detect patient lung properties and adjust accordingly — reducing clinician burden and improving care, especially in high-demand situations like the COVID-19 pandemic.

Submissions are evaluated using **log loss** (also known as cross-entropy loss). For each breath_id in the test set, you must submit a probability for each possible compliance class (10, 20, 50). The log loss penalizes confident but incorrect predictions heavily, so well-calibrated probability estimates are essential. Lower log loss scores indicate better performance.

competition_description:
Ventilator Expiratory Phase Detection: Predicting the Expiratory Valve State

In mechanical ventilation, precise control of airflow depends on accurately understanding the state of the ventilator's valves at every moment. The expiratory valve (u_out) controls whether air is being released from the patient's lungs — a critical binary signal that governs the breathing cycle. Misclassifying this state could have significant implications for understanding and simulating ventilator behavior in a clinical setting.

In this competition, your task is to predict the binary state of the expiratory valve (u_out) — whether it is open (1) or closed (0) — based on sensor readings and lung attributes collected during simulated ventilator sessions. You will work with time-series data from simulated patients with varying lung compliance and resistance characteristics. Features include time-step information, inspiratory valve control inputs, and measured airway pressure, among others.

This challenge is inspired by the broader effort to develop high-quality mechanical ventilation simulators that can generalize across diverse patient lung profiles. description:
Ventilator Expiratory Phase Detection: Predicting the Expiratory Valve State

In mechanical ventilation, precise control of airflow depends on accurately understanding the state of the ventilator's valves at every moment. The expiratory valve (u_out) controls whether air is being released from the patient's lungs — a critical binary signal that governs the breathing cycle. Misclassifying this state could have significant implications for understanding and simulating ventilator behavior in a clinical setting.

In this competition, your task is to predict the binary state of the expiratory valve (u_out) — whether it is open (1) or closed (0) — based on sensor readings and lung attributes collected during simulated ventilator sessions. You will work with time-series data from simulated patients with varying lung compliance and resistance characteristics. Features include time-step information, inspiratory valve control inputs, and measured airway pressure, among others.

This challenge is inspired by the broader effort to develop high-quality mechanical ventilation simulators that can generalize across diverse patient lung profiles. By accurately detecting the expiratory phase of the breathing cycle, participants will contribute to building more robust and interpretable ventilator control models — ultimately helping reduce the burden on clinicians and expanding access to life-saving ventilator treatments.

Submissions are evaluated using the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). For each breath time-step in the test set, you must predict the probability that the expiratory valve is open (u_out = 1). The AUC score measures the model's ability to discriminate between the expiratory (u_out = 1) and inspiratory (u_out = 0) phases across all prediction thresholds. A score of 1.0 represents a perfect classifier, while 0.5 represents random guessing.
